## Objectives {.unnumbered}

This lab accompanies the Week 6 notes, [*Data Visualisation Principles*](https://soton-fds.github.io/week06.html).

- Be able to map variables from data frames to aesthetics in `ggplot2`.
- Use common geometries (points, lines, bars, histograms and box plots).
- Use scales and coordinates, for example to zoom in on part of a plot or use a log scale.
- Summarise data before plotting to reveal patterns, such as trends hidden by seasonal variation.
- Recognise and avoid misleading plots.

When you have finished the lab, there are more questions on the same data in `lab_06_practice.qmd`, including themes, facets, colourblind-safe palettes and violin plots.

### Task 1: Temperature Trends

The file `data/MET Office Weather Data.csv` contains monthly weather observations from 36 stations in the UK between 1853 and 2020.
The fields included are:

- **year**: Year in which the measurements were taken
- **month**: Month in which the measurements were taken
- **tmax**: Mean daily maximum temperature (°C)
- **tmin**: Mean daily minimum temperature (°C)
- **af**: Days of air frost recorded that month (days)
- **rain**: Total rainfall (mm)
- **sun**: Total sunshine duration (hours)
- **station**: Station location where measurement was recorded

The year and month are stored as integers. The first cell below reads the data and adds a new column called `date` using the `lubridate` `make_date` function.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
met <- read_csv("data/MET Office Weather Data.csv")
met <- met |>
    mutate(date = make_date(year, month, 1))
```

- [ ] Produce a line plot showing how the maximum temperature in July recorded in the station in Southampton has changed over time. Add nice labels to your plot.
- [ ] There appears to be a break in the plotted line. Work out where it is by using `coord_cartesian` to zoom in on the $x$ axis, and then check the dataset to identify the root cause. (Hint: look at the `xlim` argument of `coord_cartesian`. The $x$ axis shows dates, so the limits need to be dates too.)

::: {.solution}

Below, find the plot.
```{r}
met |>
    filter(station == "southampton" & month == 7) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = tmax)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(
        x = "Date",
        y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "July maximum temperatures in Southampton"
    )
```
In the full plot there is a short gap in the line just after 1940, but it is hard to see exactly where it starts and ends.
Zooming in on the $x$ axis to 1925–1950 makes it much clearer:
```{r}
met |>
    filter(station == "southampton" & month == 7) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = tmax)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(
        x = "Date",
        y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "July maximum temperatures in Southampton"
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(ymd("1925-01-01"), ymd("1950-12-31")))
```

The gap lies between 1940 and 1945, so we can filter the dataset to just those years to see the root cause:

```{r}
met |> filter(station == "southampton" & month == 7 & year >= 1940 & year <= 1945)
```

The break is due to an `NA` value of `tmax` in 1941: the row for July 1941 exists, but the maximum temperature was not recorded.
`geom_line` cannot draw a line to a missing value, so it leaves a gap, rather than joining 1940 directly to 1942.

:::

Next we look at every month of the year, not just July, at four stations.

- [ ] Produce a scatter plot of the maximum temperature `tmax` against `date` for every month in Southampton, Oxford, Sheffield and Paisley. Colour the points by station.
- [ ] Look up the function `geom_smooth`. Use the function to overlay a smooth trend line on the points. Make sure the line is visible by adjusting the `alpha` property on `geom_point`.
- [ ] What does the line tell you about the trend of historical maximum temperatures?

::: {.solution}
The next plot shows a scatter plot by station:

```{r}
stations <- c("southampton", "oxford", "sheffield", "paisley")
met |>
    filter(station %in% stations) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = tmax, colour = station)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_smooth() +
    labs(
        x = "Date",
        y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "Monthly maximum temperatures"
    )
```

`geom_smooth()` prints a message saying which method it used.
Unlike the straight `method = "lm"` lines in the Week 6 notes, here it has fitted a flexible curve (`method = 'gam'`), which can bend to follow the data.
The grey band around each line shows the uncertainty in the fitted curve (a confidence interval); it is narrow here because there is a lot of data.
Lowering `alpha` makes the individual points faint, so the lines stand out.

The smooth lines rise slightly at each station, which hints at an increasing trend. But it is hard to be sure from this plot.
Because every month of the year is included, the points at each station span a band about 20°C tall (cold winters to warm summers), and any long-term change is small by comparison.

:::

The plot above mixes together every month of the year, so the seasonal cycle hides the long-term trend.
Averaging over each year removes the seasonal cycle, since every (complete) year contains one of each month.

- [ ] For each of Southampton, Oxford, Sheffield and Paisley, compute the mean `tmax` in each year. Plot these annual means against `year` as a line plot, coloured by station, and add a smooth trend line. Is the trend easier to see now?
- [ ] Some of the annual means look suspicious. Which years have the lowest and highest annual means? How many months of data is each annual mean based on? (Hint: how would you count the *non-missing* values of a column inside `summarise`?)
- [ ] Redraw the plot using only years with a complete set of 12 months. Roughly how much have annual mean maximum temperatures risen at these stations?

::: {.solution}

We compute the annual means, and also count how many months of `tmax` each mean is based on, since we will need this below:

```{r}
annual <- met |>
    filter(station %in% stations) |>
    group_by(station, year) |>
    summarise(
        mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
        n_months = sum(!is.na(tmax)),
        .groups = "drop"
    )

annual |>
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, colour = station)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_smooth() +
    labs(
        x = "Year",
        y = "Annual mean maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "Annual mean maximum temperatures"
    )
```

The $y$ axis now covers a few degrees rather than 25, and the upward trend is much easier to see.
But there are some odd spikes, particularly at the ends of the records.
Sorting by `mean_tmax` shows the most extreme years:

```{r}
annual |> arrange(mean_tmax) |> head(5)
annual |> arrange(desc(mean_tmax)) |> head(5)
```

The coldest "year" in the data is Paisley in 2011, but that mean is based on only 3 months of data; the warmest is Oxford in 2019, based on only 5 months.
An annual mean from a partial year depends on *which* months are present: a year containing only winter months will look very cold.
Using `na.rm = TRUE` made the `mean` calculation work, but it did not make the answer meaningful.
(Where a station has no `tmax` values at all for a year, `mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)` returns `NaN`, "not a number", and `ggplot` drops these rows with a warning.)

Keeping only complete years:

```{r}
annual |>
    filter(n_months == 12) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, colour = station)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_smooth() +
    labs(
        x = "Year",
        y = "Annual mean maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "Annual mean maximum temperatures (complete years only)"
    )
```

Oxford and Sheffield warm by about 2°C over their records, most of it since around 1980.
Southampton warms by about 1°C, more steadily, although its record stops in 2000.
Paisley's record is too short (1959–2011) to say much on its own.
Note that when we *filter out* incomplete years, `geom_line` simply joins the remaining points, so there is no break in the line where a year is missing.
Compare this with the July plot at the start of this task, where an `NA` value produced a visible gap.

:::

### Task 2: Rainfall

- [ ] Produce a bar chart showing how many monthly records there are for each station, using `geom_bar()`. Then produce the same chart using `count()` and `geom_col()`. (Hint: to make the station names readable, add `theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))` to your plot.)

::: {.solution}

`geom_bar()` counts the rows in each category for us, so we only need to give it an `x` aesthetic.

```{r}
met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station)) +
    geom_bar() +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Number of monthly records",
        title = "Number of monthly records by station"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Alternatively we can count the rows ourselves with `count()`, which creates a column `n`.
The bar heights are then already in the data, so we use `geom_col()`:

```{r}
met |>
    count(station) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = n)) +
    geom_col() +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Number of monthly records",
        title = "Number of monthly records by station"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

The two plots are identical.

:::

- [ ] Produce a bar chart showing the average rainfall (across all months and years) for the 5 stations with the highest average rainfall.
- [ ] Now make a *deliberately misleading* version of this plot, which suggests that Cwmystwyth gets several times as much rain as Stornoway. Which of the principles in the Week 6 notes does your plot break? How could a reader spot the trick?

::: {.solution}

We first compute the mean rainfall at each station with `group_by` and `summarise`.
Because we have already computed the height of each bar, we use `geom_col()`; `geom_bar()` would instead count the rows in each category.
To keep only the five wettest stations, we sort the summarised data with `arrange(desc(...))` and keep the first five rows with `head(5)` *before* passing it to `ggplot`.

```{r}
met |>
    group_by(station) |>
    summarise(mean_rainfall = mean(rain, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(mean_rainfall)) |>
    head(5) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = mean_rainfall)) +
    geom_col() +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Mean monthly rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Mean monthly rainfall at the five wettest stations"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Cwmystwyth has a mean monthly rainfall of about 150 mm and Stornoway about 100 mm, so Cwmystwyth is only about 1.5 times as wet.
To make the difference look much bigger, we can zoom in on the $y$ axis with `coord_cartesian`, as we did in Task 1, so that the bars no longer start at zero:

```{r}
met |>
    group_by(station) |>
    summarise(mean_rainfall = mean(rain, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(mean_rainfall)) |>
    head(5) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = mean_rainfall)) +
    geom_col() +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(95, 150)) +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Mean monthly rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Mean monthly rainfall at the five wettest stations"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

The Cwmystwyth bar is now around seven times as tall as the Stornoway bar.
This breaks the first principle, "Be honest with scales": we read a bar chart by comparing the *lengths* of the bars, so the value axis should start at zero.
It is the same trick as the welfare chart in the Week 6 notes.
Nothing in the plot is technically false: a careful reader can spot the trick by checking where the $y$ axis starts.
But most readers will judge the bar lengths rather than read the axis.

(Setting `scale_y_continuous(limits = c(95, 150))` instead does not work: `ggplot` removes any bar that extends outside the scale limits, and since every bar starts at zero, all five disappear with a warning.
`coord_cartesian` zooms in on the plot *after* the bars have been drawn, instead.)

:::

Bar charts of averages hide how much the rainfall varies from month to month, so next we look at its *distribution*.

- [ ] Look up how to produce a box plot with `ggplot`, and produce a box plot of rainfall at each station. Are there any outliers at the low end? Why not?

::: {.solution}

Box plots use `geom_boxplot()`, with the grouping variable on one axis and the numeric variable on the other.

```{r}
met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = rain)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall by station"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

By default, the whiskers extend up to 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) beyond the box, and any points outside them are drawn as outliers.
There are plenty of high outliers (very wet months), but no low outliers at all.
Rainfall cannot be negative, and at every station the lower whisker limit (the lower quartile minus 1.5 times the IQR) is below zero, so no value can fall beneath it.

:::

- [ ] Plot a histogram of monthly rainfall across all stations. Experiment with the `bins` argument. How would you describe the shape of the distribution?
- [ ] Redraw the histogram with a logarithmic $x$ axis (see the Week 6 notes). What happens to the shape? Read the warning messages carefully, and compare the number of rows removed with the previous histogram. Which months have been dropped, and why?

::: {.solution}

A histogram needs only an `x` aesthetic: `geom_histogram()` divides the $x$ axis into bins and counts the rows in each one.

```{r}
met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = rain)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
    labs(
        x = "Monthly rainfall (mm)",
        y = "Number of months",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall across all stations"
    )
```

With too few bins (say 5) the shape is lost; with too many (say 500) the histogram becomes noisy.
Something in the range 30–100 works well here.

The distribution is strongly *right-skewed*: half of all months have between about 40 and 95 mm of rain (the median is 63 mm), but there is a long tail of very wet months reaching up to 569 mm (Eskdalemuir, December 2015).
On the left the distribution stops sharply at zero, since rainfall cannot be negative.

For the log scale, we add a scale transformation, as in the Week 6 notes:

```{r}
met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = rain)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
    scale_x_continuous(transform = "log10") +
    labs(
        x = "Monthly rainfall (mm, log scale)",
        y = "Number of months",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall across all stations"
    )
```

The log scale stretches out small values and squashes large ones.
The long tail of wet months is pulled in, and the distribution is now *left*-skewed instead, with a tail of unusually dry months (below 10 mm).
So the log scale does not make the distribution symmetric, but it does make the dry months, which were squashed against zero before, much easier to see.

There are two warnings.
The first says that the log transformation "introduced infinite values", and the second that 1503 rows were removed, compared with 1498 for the original histogram.
The 1498 are the rows where `rain` is `NA`.
The extra 5 are months with *zero* rainfall, because $\log_{10}(0) = -\infty$ cannot be plotted:

```{r}
met |> filter(rain == 0)
```

Some UK months really have been this dry, so these are probably genuine observations rather than errors, yet the log scale drops them from the plot.
It is always worth reading warnings like this rather than ignoring them.

:::
